web_title: 6. The Balance Sheet, the Cash Flow & Who Owns the Company
question: Does the money on the balance sheet work for the business, and does the cash behind the profit arrive on time?

epigraph.quote: Now basically cash flow is not a true reflection of anything.
epigraph.author: Shazad Rustomji, Chairman, CEO and Managing Director, Q2 and H1 FY27 earnings call, 19 November 2026 [36]

web_blocks.html: The earlier chapters told the operating story in words. This chapter puts the five-year financials, the September 2026 balance sheet, the monitoring agency findings, the Maharashtra GST search, and the ownership trail side by side. The balance sheet shows where the raised equity actually went. The cash flow shows whether reported profit turned into cash. The shareholding table shows who now bears the risk.

web_blocks.title: The profit and loss, five years and a trailing year

web_blocks.html: Start with the multi-year income statement to see how sales growth compares with margin stability. Stallion grew turnover steadily after FY21, yet operating margins moved in wide waves rather than compounding smoothly.

web_blocks.caption: Stallion: profit and loss, March 2021 to March 2026 and trailing twelve months (₹ crore, Screener) [14]
web_blocks.takeaway: Sales rose about 3.7 times between March 2021 and March 2026. The operating margin moved between 8% and 18% across the years shown, so margins never climbed steadily with scale.

web_blocks.html: Sales climbed from ₹118 crore to ₹431 crore in five years, and net profit rose from ₹10 crore to ₹44 crore [14]. Those gains are real, yet the path was volatile. Sales nearly stalled in FY24 at ₹233 crore, and profit fell to ₹15 crore that year. Trailing twelve-month sales reached ₹472 crore with reported net profit of ₹43 crore, reflecting June’s strong quarter offset by September’s ₹2.45 crore slump [14].

web_blocks.title: The balance sheet changed in one year

web_blocks.html: Two equity raises in fourteen months transformed Stallion’s balance sheet from a small leveraged distributor into a ₹711 crore net-worth vehicle. Look closely at how fast that raised cash moved out of bank accounts between March and September 2026.

web_blocks.caption: Stallion: balance sheet, March 2021 to September 2026 (₹ crore, Screener; Total Liabilities includes equity) [14]
web_blocks.takeaway: Equity rose from ₹301 crore in March 2025 to ₹681 crore in March 2026 and ₹711 crore by September 2026, while borrowings stayed low.

web_blocks.html: Total equity rose from ₹300.84 crore at March 2025 to ₹680.60 crore at March 2026 [1]. It reached ₹711.15 crore at 30 September 2026. The February 2026 rights issue drove most of that jump (₹363.93 crore gross; ₹336.02 crore net in FY26 cash flow), alongside retained earnings and ESOP reserves [1][38]. The H1 FY27 balance sheet shows that capital leaving the bank rapidly. Cash and bank balances fell ₹141.97 crore, from ₹433.67 crore at March 2026 to ₹291.70 crore at September 2026 [1][36]. Fixed Assets plus Capital Work-in-Progress more than doubled, from ₹65.60 crore to ₹145.97 crore (Fixed Assets ₹56 crore, CWIP ₹90 crore) [14][36]. Short-term borrowings fell from ₹34.01 crore to ₹6.47 crore [14][36]. Meanwhile, Other Current Assets surged 7.2 times, from ₹22.42 crore to ₹160.88 crore. Most of that jump reflects ₹129 crore of capital advances to Bhilwara’s civil EPC contractor plus supplier advances [1][14][36][38].

web_blocks.caption: Major balance-sheet lines, March 2025, March 2026 (audited) [1], and September 2026 (H1 FY27 limited review) [14][36][38]
rows: Fell ₹141.97 crore in six months as project spending and EPC advances ramped
More than doubled in H1 FY27 (CWIP reached ₹90 crore)

Both eased in H1 FY27, while trade payables rose from ₹18.15 crore to ₹49.75 crore

web_blocks.takeaway: Rights-issue cash is nearly committed: combined with ₹129 crore of EPC advances and rising CWIP, cash balances fell ₹142 crore in six months and management now anticipates raising another ₹200 crore [36][38].

web_blocks.html: That single line—Other Current Assets jumping from ₹22.42 crore to ₹160.88 crore in six months—is the sharpest balance-sheet shift in the H1 FY27 filing [36][38]. Until those ₹129 crore of contractor advances convert into verified, commissioned chemical reactors, they represent counterparty and execution exposure rather than productive steel in the ground.

Accounting profit means little in a working-capital-heavy chemical distributor unless cash reaches the bank. Stallion’s six-year cash-flow statement shows why cash conversion remains the core weak link in the business model.

web_blocks.caption: Stallion: cash flow, March 2021 to March 2026 (₹ crore, Screener) [24]
web_blocks.takeaway: Operating cash was negative in FY24 and FY25, turned positive once in FY26, and relapsed to −₹39.17 crore in H1 FY27 [1][24][36].

web_blocks.html: Operating cash flow was negative in FY24 (−₹73 crore) and FY25 (−₹13.43 crore) [1][24]. It turned positive once in FY26 at ₹39.36 crore [1][24]. Then it relapsed immediately to −₹39.17 crore (−₹3,916.92 lakh) in H1 FY27 despite ₹30.53 crore of pre-tax profit [36]. That leaves cumulative six-and-a-half-year operating cash flow deeply negative. On the 19 November 2026 call, the Chairman and CEO dismissed cash-flow scrutiny outright. He stated verbatim that “cash flow is not a true reflection of anything” [36].

Investing cash flow in FY26 (−₹253 crore) was mostly ₹205.13 crore of fixed deposits alongside ₹49.31 crore of capex [23]. By November 2026, both equity pools were largely spent or committed. CARE Ratings reported ₹160.33 crore used out of the ₹160.73 crore IPO fresh issue [37]. Infomerics reported ₹278.29 crore used out of the ₹363.93 crore Rights Issue by 30 September, and management said roughly ₹50 crore remained in November [36][38]. Infomerics also flagged ₹36.00 crore (9.9% of gross rights proceeds) spent on issue expenses [38]. In Q2 FY27, ₹78.00 crore went as advances to civil EPC contractor Pansen Engineering India Pvt Ltd on a ₹269.76 crore cost-plus 10% contract. Infomerics could not map those payments to individual invoices because invoices follow structure completion [38]. Even after raising ₹524.66 crore in two issues over 14 months, management flagged a fresh ~₹200 crore external funding need via QIP, preferential issue, debentures, or debt [36]. Combined gross outlays across ₹150 crore of R-32 start-up working capital, ₹40 crore of Bhilwara overrun, ₹10 to ₹15 crore for Mambattu, and ₹200 crore of HFO capex total ₹400 to ₹405 crore [36][37]. That ~₹200 crore incremental external raise bridges the net shortfall alongside roughly ₹50 crore of remaining rights-issue cash, internal operating accruals, the unused ₹120 crore bank overdraft facility, and phased late-2027 HFO capex timing (deferred until three to five months after Bhilwara R-32 stabilizes) [36].

web_blocks.caption: FY26 cash sources and uses, largest items (₹ crore, audited) [1][23]
rows: Net proceeds of the rights issue
Property, plant and equipment, intangibles and work in progress
web_blocks.takeaway: These were the largest FY26 lines [23]. In H1 FY27, cash and deposits drew down by ₹141.97 crore as unmapped EPC advances and CWIP surged [36][38].

web_blocks.html: Put the two halves together and the capital cycle becomes stark. Stallion raised ₹524.66 crore of fresh public equity in fourteen months [36][37][38]. It spent 9.9% of the rights issue on issue expenses alone [38]. It advanced ₹129 crore on a cost-plus 10% civil contract before invoicing [38]. Yet it still needs roughly ₹200 crore in incremental external funding (alongside remaining rights cash, accruals, the ₹120 crore overdraft, and deferred HFO timing) across ₹400–₹405 crore of combined uses before Bhilwara sells a single kilogram of R-32 [36][37].

web_blocks.title: Internal controls, monitoring-agency flags & Maharashtra GST search

web_blocks.html: Two governance and tax disclosures omitted from the baseline draft demand close balance-sheet attention. First, CARE Ratings’ 14 November 2026 IPO Monitoring Agency report carried a formal qualification (“Deviation from the objects: Yes”) on ₹0.40 crore paid from company cash instead of liquidating an IPO fixed deposit [37]. CARE also flagged commingling of IPO proceeds in routine current accounts, with ₹2.49 crore claimed as reimbursements [37]. Prior excess issue expenses of ₹3.99 crore had been misclassified under working capital in management and CA certificates. Shareholders retroactively regularized that misclassification via a 3 June 2026 special resolution, alongside a ₹7.80 crore land purchase replacing a ₹7.67 crore warehouse [37]. CARE further warned that overspending on Objects 1 and 2 reduced funds left for Mambattu, risking object viability [37]. Both Khalapur and Mambattu also breached their June 2026 extended timelines without further shareholder approval [37].

Second, on 15 October 2026, Stallion filed a Regulation 30 notice on a tax search [39]. Maharashtra State GST officials (Investigation-C, Mumbai) inspected and searched its Mumbai registered office under Section 67 of the MGST Act from 9 to 14 October 2026 [39]. Authorities cited five Input Tax Credit contraventions [39]. These covered inadmissible credit on IPO Offer-for-Sale expenses (Section 17(2)), ineligible Rajasthan Rights Issue credit (Section 20), credit from a cancelled supplier, improper Input Service Distributor allocation (Section 20), and blocked GSTR-3B credit (Section 17(5)) [39]. Stallion voluntarily reversed credits and paid tax and interest. Management reported no material operational impact, but it did not disclose the rupee amount paid [39].

web_blocks.title: Returns on capital, and why the ratio fell

web_blocks.html: When equity expands faster than operating profit and working capital stays heavy, returns on capital compress mechanically. Stallion’s six-year efficiency table traces that slide from peak trading returns down to low-teens capital returns.

web_blocks.caption: Stallion: return and working-capital ratios, March 2021 to March 2026 (Screener) [24]
web_blocks.takeaway: Return on capital employed fell from 55% in March 2022 to 12% in March 2026, and equity dilution plus delayed plant commissioning continue to weigh on returns [14][24].

web_blocks.html: Return on capital employed fell from 55% in March 2022 to 12% in March 2026 (11.8% on Screener’s live card) [14][24]. Screener’s return on equity is 8.93% (8.37% on TradingView), with a three-year average of 11.4% [14][32]. Bhilwara R-32 and Mambattu will deliver zero FY27 revenue even though net worth has already expanded to ₹711.15 crore [36]. With another ₹200 crore raise under review, returns on capital face prolonged dilution drag until new plants earn commercial returns [36].

web_blocks.title: Who owns the company now—the 20-point promoter drop decoded

web_blocks.html: Ownership changes often speak louder than investor presentations. The shareholding trail from March 2025 to September 2026 shows promoter stake dropping more than twenty percentage points while institutional ownership faded and retail investors took majority control.

web_blocks.caption: Shareholding pattern, March 2025 to September 2026, with shareholder count (Screener and SEBI SAST filings) [15][40]
web_blocks.takeaway: Promoter ownership dropped 20.10 percentage points via two verified steps: open-market sales of 3.06% in Oct–Nov 2025 [40], followed by minimal promoter participation in the Feb 2026 rights issue (17.04-point dilution), while institutional holding shrank to 1.88% and public retail crossed 50% [15].

web_blocks.html: The prior draft left the 20.10 percentage-point drop in promoter ownership unverified. Exchange filings now establish both steps cleanly. First, a SEBI SAST Regulation 29(2) filing dated 7 November 2025 showed open-market selling by the founder [40]. Chairman and CEO Shazad Sheriar Rustomji sold 24,28,987 shares (3.06% of equity) across four sessions from 29 October to 4 November 2025. That sale cut promoter stake from 67.90% to 64.84% [40]. Second, the February 2026 Rights Issue allotted 3,67,60,483 new shares, lifting share capital from 7.93 crore to 11.61 crore shares [15]. Promoter stake diluted another 17.04 points to 47.80% and stayed there through September 2026, with zero shares pledged [15]. Promoters subscribed to only a small fraction of their rights entitlement, while public investors absorbed most of the issue [15]. Institutional ownership (FIIs 0.28% plus DIIs 1.60%) sits at just 1.88%, while public retail ownership reached 50.33% across 66,734 shareholders [15]. Separately, H1 FY27 ESOP grants of 15,86,505 options at ₹10 face value (one-year vesting) add 1.37% potential dilution on top of the signaled ₹200 crore raise [36].

web_blocks.region_era: United States, FY2018 to FY2019, generic drugs after a distribution partner’s agreement expired
web_blocks.mechanism: One product sold through a partner was about 37% of sales. The partner agreement expired and was not renewed, receivables ran above the company’s own expected range, and gross margin fell in the same year as a large impairment and loss.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: The partner’s product sales were $253.1 million (37% of net sales) in fiscal 2018 and $202.5 million (31%) in fiscal 2019 [29]. Gross margin fell from 42% to 37%, the operating loss was $262.3 million including $375.4 million of impairment, and net income of $28.7 million became a net loss of $272.1 million [28].
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: A single-product business with a long cash cycle can move from profit to a large loss in one year. Stallion’s R-32 is its main product, its cash conversion cycle is about 180 days, and H1 FY27 operating cash flow just relapsed to negative −₹39.17 crore [24][36].

web_blocks.title: NARRATOR’S REFLECTION
paragraphs: Read the balance sheet next to the monitoring reports and ownership trail. Stallion raised ₹524.66 crore in fresh equity across two issues in 14 months [36][37][38]. Promoters sold 3.06% beforehand and took only a small slice of the rights issue [40]. Yet both cash pools are nearly spent, and management now eyes another ₹200 crore raise [36].

Add CARE Ratings’ deviation and commingling qualification plus Infomerics’ unmapped cost-plus-10% EPC advances [37][38]. Pair those with the October 2026 GST search and the CEO’s dismissal of cash flow [36][39]. Together, they create severe governance and capital-allocation risks.

book_paragraphs: Now the balance sheet, cash flow, internal controls, and ownership—because the November 2026 filings changed this chapter more than any other. Start with the multi-year profit and loss: sales rose from 118 crore in FY21 to 431 crore in FY26, and net profit climbed from 10 crore to 44 crore. Yet operating margins swung wildly between 8% and 18%, and Q2 FY27 reported net profit collapsed to 2.45 crore.

The H1 FY27 balance sheet shows the February rights-issue cash draining rapidly out of bank accounts. Net worth expanded to 711.15 crore, Fixed Assets plus Capital Work-in-Progress more than doubled from 65.60 crore to 145.97 crore, and short-term borrowings fell from 34.01 crore to 6.47 crore. Meanwhile, cash and bank balances dropped 141.97 crore in just six months, from 433.67 crore at March 2026 down to 291.70 crore at September 2026.

Where did the rest of that money go? Look at Other Current Assets. That line exploded more than sevenfold in six months, jumping from 22.42 crore to 160.88 crore. The bulk of it—129 crore—sits in capital advances paid out to Bhilwara’s civil engineering contractor plus supplier advances. Until those advances turn into commissioned reactors running commercial refrigerant, they are counterparty exposure rather than earning assets.

That advance and working-capital drain pushed H1 FY27 operating cash flow right back to negative 39.17 crore despite 30.53 crore of pre-tax profit. That snaps FY26’s lone positive cash year and leaves cumulative six-and-a-half-year operating cash flow deeply negative. Even more jarring, when an analyst asked about the cash-flow reversal on the 19 November call, Chairman and CEO Shazad Rustomji declared that cash flow is not a true reflection of anything.

The 14 November 2026 SEBI monitoring agency reports expose serious internal-control weaknesses that the baseline dossier missed. On the 363.93 crore rights issue, Infomerics reported 278.29 crore already utilized by 30 September—including 36 crore, nearly 10% of gross proceeds, consumed by issue expenses alone. Infomerics also disclosed that civil EPC contractor Pansen Engineering India works on a cost-plus 10% contract of 269.76 crore and receives large on-account advances (78 crore in Q2 alone) before raising invoices, preventing the monitoring agency from mapping individual cash disbursements to invoices.

On the 160.73 crore IPO proceeds, CARE Ratings issued an explicit qualification—Deviation from the objects: Yes—for substituting company funds instead of liquidating an IPO fixed deposit, flagged commingling of IPO proceeds in routine current accounts across 2.49 crore of reimbursements, and cited 3.99 crore of excess issue expenses previously misclassified under working capital. CARE Ratings also warned that overspending on working capital and Khalapur left less funding for Mambattu, potentially affecting object viability, while both Khalapur and Mambattu breached even their June 2026 extended timelines without fresh shareholder approval.

One month earlier, on 15 October 2026, Stallion disclosed a six-day Maharashtra State GST Section 67 inspection and search at its Mumbai registered office. Officials flagged five separate Input Tax Credit contraventions: inadmissible credit on IPO Offer-for-Sale expenses, ineligible Rajasthan rights-issue credit, credit from a cancelled supplier, improper Input Service Distributor allocation, and blocked Section 17(5) credit. Stallion paid tax and interest voluntarily without disclosing the rupee outflow.

Step back and look at the capital cycle. Despite raising 524.66 crore in fresh equity across two public issues in fourteen months, both cash pools are virtually exhausted, with only about 50 crore of rights funds unspent in November. Combined gross outlays across 150 crore of R-32 start-up working capital, 40 crore of Bhilwara cost overruns, Mambattu’s 10 to 15 crore shortfall, and 200 crore of future HFO capex total 400 to 405 crore. Management’s signaled 200 crore represents the incremental external raise expected alongside roughly 50 crore of remaining rights cash, internal operating accruals, the unused 120 crore bank overdraft facility, and phased late-2027 HFO timing. Meanwhile, ROCE sits near 12% and ROE under 9% with zero FY27 revenue from Bhilwara or Mambattu to lift returns.

Finally, exchange filings decode the 20.1 percentage-point promoter stake drop left unexplained in the earlier draft. First, SEBI SAST filings show Chairman and CEO Shazad Rustomji sold 24.29 lakh shares—3.06% of equity—in the open market across late October and early November 2025, cutting promoter ownership from 67.90% to 64.84%. Second, when the February 2026 rights issue issued 3.68 crore new shares, promoter stake diluted another 17.04 points to 47.80% with zero shares pledged. That proves promoters subscribed to only a small fraction of their rights entitlement while public retail investors absorbed the issue, pushing public ownership to 50.33% across 66,734 shareholders while institutional ownership shrank to just 1.88%. Add 15.87 lakh deep-discount ESOPs at 10 rupees exercise price and a signaled third capital raise, and serial dilution has steadily outpaced profit growth.

For the failure base rate, Lannett Company in the United States remains the sharp cautionary mirror: a single-product distributor with a stretched cash cycle can swing from solid profit to a massive loss in a single year when a core partner or spread breaks. Keep three hard lines on your desk every quarter: operating cash flow, unmapped EPC advances and fresh equity dilution, and whether Bhilwara actually stabilizes by May 2027 without another overrun.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR’S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Keep a single page with three lines: operating cash flow, unmapped contractor advances and equity raises, and the promoter stake. Read it each quarter. Governance and capital-allocation erosion rarely announce themselves in one headline; they accumulate across footnotes until the balance sheet forces a third equity raise.
